(2) The Drinfeld half-plane: H^1_ét(Ω_Dr,Q_p(1)) ≅ (St^{cont}_{Q_p})^* (Theorem 1.7, Drinfeld's theorem, proved here by Kummer theory) and the exact sequence 0 → O(Ω_Dr)/C → H^1_proét(Ω_Dr,Q_p(1)) → (St^{lisse}_{Q_p})^* → 0 with its de Rham companion (Theorem 1.8 and Corollary 1.9), together with the description of O(Ω_Dr)^*/C^*, Ω^1(Ω_Dr) and H^1_dR(Ω_Dr) by Steinberg duals (Propositions 1.5 and 1.6). (3) The tower: an equivariant semi-stable model of M^ϖ_n over a finite extension of F for every n (Proposition A.1), the compactly supported comparison H^1_{dR,c}(LT^ϖ_∞) ≅ H^1_{dR,c}(M^ϖ_∞) with both sides admissible as G-modules (Theorem 4.1), the Galois-cohomology computation H^i_cont(K,O(X̂)) for a perfectoid Galois covering (Lemma 4.4, Proposition 4.5), the vanishing [O(M^ϖ_n)^*]^{G_j} = 0 and [O(LT^ϖ_j)^*]^{Ǧ_n} = 0 (Proposition 4.8), the decomposition H^1_{dR,c}(M^ϖ_∞) = ⊕_{M∈ΦN^ϖ} JL_1(M) ⊗ WD_1(M) ⊗ LL_1(M)^∨ (Theorem 5.8), the Hyodo–Kato and de Rham computations Hom_Ǧ(JL(M), H^1_HK(M^ϖ_∞)) ≅ M̆ ⊗̂ LL(M)^* (Theorem 5.10 = Theorem 0.4) and the fundamental diagram for the tower (Theorem 5.11 = Theorem 0.8). (4) The global method that proves them: p-adic uniformisation, the Frobenius reciprocity of Lemma 5.6 for D^alg(G)-Fréchet spaces, π-isotypic Fréchet spaces with the Jacobson-density stability theorem (Definition 5.13, Propositions 5.14 and 5.16), and Proposition 5.12. Import the period sheaves from PadicHodgeTheory P8, Hyodo–Kato from CrystallineCohomology CR.6, the semi-stable comparison from CohomologyComparisons CP.4, perfectoid geometry from PerfectoidSpaces P1–P2, the two towers and non-abelian Lubin–Tate from EndoscopicTransferAndUnitaryTraceComparison ET.6a, Banach–Colmez spaces from VectorBundlesAndIsocrystals VB3, the Shimura curves and their uniformisation from HilbertModularVarietiesAndShimuraCurves R18.5, local–global compatibility from AutomorphicGaloisRepresentations R19.4/R19.5, and stable reduction of algebraic curves from the Tau Ceti stable reduction roadmap. Do not plan the p-adic local Langlands correspondence here: it is the Part II below.

routes.title: P-adic local Langlands for GL₂(Q_p), Part II: the geometric realisation in the Drinfeld tower
routes.reason: The parent roadmap constructs the correspondence V ↦ Π(V) through Colmez's functor (R30.3) and the representation categories it lives in (R30.2), and R30.6 exports the local results consumed by modularity lifting. What this paper adds is in exactly that direction and in no other: a geometric construction of Π(V) for the supercuspidal V of weights 0 and 1, as the multiplicity space of V in the p-adic étale cohomology of the Drinfeld tower, together with the representation theory that the construction needs (the Steinberg representation in its smooth, continuous and locally analytic forms, the representations W_{M,L}, the classification of the V that can occur and the finite length of the multiplicity spaces). It is new layers of the parent, not a new roadmap, and not a source of an existing layer: no stage of the parent mentions the tower.
routes.brief: Final theorems. (1) Theorem 0.2 (= Corollary 2.16): for V an absolutely irreducible L-representation of Gal_{Q_p} of dimension ≥ 2, Hom_{W_{Q_p}}(V, L ⊗ H^1_ét(M_∞,Q_p(1))) = JL(V) ⊗_L Π(V)^* if V is supercuspidal of dimension 2 with Hodge–Tate weights 0 and 1, and 0 otherwise. (2) The two ingredients that make it a statement about the correspondence: Proposition 2.12, that H^1_ét(M_n,L(1)) is the space of G-bounded vectors of H^1_proét(M_n,L(1)), and the Breuil–Strauch conjecture in the form of Proposition 2.9, W_{M,L} = (Π(V_{M,L})^an)^*, proved by Dospinescu–Le Bras and quoted here. (3) The classification statements: V_{M,L} = Ker(X^+_st(M) → C ⊗ (M_dR/L)) is supercuspidal of dimension 2 with weights 0 and 1 and every such representation is V_{M,L} for a unique pair (M,L) (Colmez–Fontaine); Proposition 2.5 and Lemma 2.7, that Hom_{Gal_F}(V, X_st(M)) = Hom_{WD_F}(M[−1]^*, D_pst(V^*)) and that for dim V = 2 it is at most one-dimensional and forces D_pst(V) ≅ M[−1]; and Remark 2.6, which determines exactly which filtrations occur for a general F and is where the restriction to F = Q_p comes from. (4) Theorem 2.15: Hom(V, H^1_ét[M]) ≠ 0 if and only if some V_{M,L} is a quotient of V, and Π_M(V) = Hom(V,H^1_ét[M])^* is admissible of finite length with Jordan–Hölder factors among the Π(V_{M,L}); with the linear-algebra Lemma 2.18 that the proof needs. (5) The representation theory to plan alongside: the smooth, continuous and locally F-analytic Steinberg representations of GL_2(F) and their duals, with St^{cont}_L the universal unitary completion of St^{lisse}_L and (St^{cont}_L)^* the G-bounded part of (St^{lisse}_L)^*; the multiplicity functors Z ↦ Z[M] = Hom_{L[Ǧ]}(JL(M), L ⊗ Z); and the construction of W'_{M,L} and W_{M,L} out of the de Rham row of the fundamental diagram. Import Colmez's functor and the universal completion theorem from R30.2/R30.3, the classical local Langlands and Jacquet–Langlands correspondences from GL2AutomorphicRepresentationsAndTransfer R16.3/R17.1, Banach–Colmez spaces from VectorBundlesAndIsocrystals VB3, and the whole cohomological input — the fundamental diagram and the cohomology of the tower — from the roadmap proposed above; plan none of it again. Record as expectations, not targets: that Π_geo(V_{M,L}) = Hom(V_{M,L},H^1_ét[M])^* is the right object for a p-adic local Langlands correspondence for GL_2(F) with F ≠ Q_p (Remarks 2.11 and 2.14), and everything in Remark 0.3 about the completed tower, Scholze's functor and a p-adic Jacquet–Langlands correspondence.

routes.reason: ET.6a is the two-tower cohomological realization in mixed characteristic: it constructs the Lubin–Tate tower with its GL_n(E), D^× and W_E actions, the Drinfeld tower with its level maps and period morphisms, the infinite-level moduli description and the Scholze–Weinstein duality isomorphism, and proves the supercuspidal isotypic realization — that is, non-abelian Lubin–Tate theory. This paper is a source for all four: it uses the equivariance of the Scholze–Weinstein isomorphism ‘pleinement’, it consumes the ℓ-adic isotypic decomposition twice (to prove the de Rham analogue in Theorem 5.8 and to bound invariants under compact open subgroups), and its Proposition 4.8 needs the explicit Gross–Hopkins coordinates, with the identity f_1f_2′ − f_2f_1′ = 2f_3, which that stage should export. Note also that this paper's Theorem 0.6 and Theorem 5.8 are the de Rham analogues of ET.6a's ℓ-adic statements, which is new mathematics and is routed below, not here.

P8 constructs the shared relative period sheaves — the integral A_inf sheaf and the rational structural, de Rham and crystalline/semi-stable period sheaves — and R06.3 attaches a potentially semi-stable Weil–Deligne parameter to a de Rham representation (Fontaine's recipe). The paper needs from P8 exactly the two fundamental four-term sequences of pro-étale sheaves, 0 → Q_p(1) → (B^+_cris)^{φ=p} → Ô → 0 and 0 → Ô(1) → B^+_dR/t² → Ô → 0, and from R06.3 the recipe in its (φ,N,Gal_F)-module form M ↦ WD(M) with the effect of the twist M[1] on the parameter.

CR.6 forms the rational Hyodo–Kato complex and proves the comparison theorem for the Hyodo–Kato to log-de-Rham map. This paper is a source for the shape that comparison must take for a non-proper curve and for a tower: an ind-Fréchet (φ,N,Gal_F)-module over Q̆_p with ι_HK: C ⊗̂ H^1_HK ≅ H^1_dR, and the identification of H^1_HK of a Stein curve as a projective limit of finite-dimensional spaces.

CP.4 constructs the B_st comparison for proper flat semi-stable formal models with the Galois, Frobenius, monodromy and filtration compatibilities. Proposition 3.12 is a direct consumer: it uses the potential semi-stability of H^1_ét of a proper curve with weights 0, −1, the identification of D_pst with Hyodo–Kato cohomology, and Fil^1 D_dR ≅ Ω^1.

PR.4 builds the syntomic/Tate-twist fibres and the comparison from generic-fibre étale cohomology to the Frobenius-fixed prismatic cohomology. The paper's §0.6.1 sketches the syntomic route to its fundamental diagram — the route that generalises to higher dimension — and Remark 0.11 needs the integral form of that comparison, up to bounded torsion; both are statements PR.4 must export.

P1 builds perfectoid Tate rings, tilts and untilts and P2 rational localisation, sheafiness and all-degree almost acyclicity on affinoid perfectoids. §4 consumes precisely the acyclicity (for the Čech computation of Lemma 4.4) and the fact that a quasi-compact rational domain in an increasing union of affinoid perfectoids is affinoid perfectoid (Proposition 4.2).

R30.2 builds the smooth mod-p, admissible unitary Banach and locally analytic categories for GL_2(Q_p) with their duals, and R30.3 Colmez's construction V ↦ Π(V). The paper is a source for the two facts about them that its argument turns on: LL(V) = Π(V)^{lisse}, and that Π(V) is the universal unitary completion of Π(V)^an, equivalently that Π(V)^* is the G-bounded part of (Π(V)^an)^* (Colmez–Dospinescu). The geometric realisation of the correspondence itself is the Part II proposed below.

R16.3 is local Langlands for GL_2 with its normalisation bridge, R17.1 the quaternionic local transfer (local Jacquet–Langlands) and R17.3 the global Jacquet–Langlands correspondence with the strong multiplicity one statements. §5 uses all three: the local ones to define LL(M) and JL(M), and the global ones to match Π̌ with Π and to know that Π̌^p_f determines Π̌_p. The paper is a good source for the definite-quaternion globalisation it needs, including Clozel's limit multiplicity input.

R19.4 proves local–global compatibility away from p and R19.5 at the coefficient prime. Proposition 5.2 is exactly their consequence for the Shimura curves of a quaternion algebra over a totally real field — Carayol's and T. Saito's theorems, in the form π_v ≅ JL(WD(ρ_{π,v})) at every finite place including v = p — combined with D_pst and D_dR and with strong multiplicity one.

R18.5 constructs the Drinfeld upper half-plane with its formal model and descent datum, identifies dual graphs and monodromy pairings, and proves the uniformisation theorem in the Shimura-curve cases. The paper is a source for the two refinements it needs: the explicit affinoid exhaustion of the half-plane with the G-equivariant reduction map to the Bruhat–Tits tree and the standard model as an iterated blow-up of P^1_{O_F}; and the uniformisation in the Boutot–Zink form, for every level of the Drinfeld tower and compatibly with the transition maps.

TB.1 builds discs, annuli, metric trees and the classification of points of a Berkovich curve, TB.2 semi-stable models, skeletons and the retraction of the analytification. Appendix A needs the non-compact theory on top of that: triangulations (semistable vertex sets), the notion of a node, the analytic skeleton as the complement of the virtual-open-disc locus, and the statement that an automorphism of the pair (X_K, S(X)) extends uniquely to the formal model — which is what makes the equivariance argument work for a non-compact M^ϖ_n.

VB3 builds Banach–Colmez geometry — the sheaf of sections of a bundle on the Fargues–Fontaine curve, its diamond representability, dimension and cohomological smoothness — of which the spaces X^+_st(M) = (B^+_cris ⊗ M)^{φ=p} are the basic positive-slope examples. The paper uses only their Dimension ([L:Q_p],2), but uses it decisively: it is what makes the multiplicity spaces of Lemma 2.7 one-dimensional and hence what pins down V_{M,L}.

A1 constructs the small étale and finite étale sites of an adic space and, for the pro-étale extension, Scholze's corrected transfinite-tower definition. The paper needs the projection ν: X_proét → X_ét and the completed structure sheaves Ô^+_X, Ô_X on it, and is a source for the warning that this is the older pro-étale site, not the one of ‘Étale cohomology of diamonds’ (its footnote 16).

gaps.detail: Two ingredients are quoted from papers that were unpublished when this one appeared. The isomorphism ~HK(X) ≅ (B^+_st ⊗̂ H^1_HK(X))^{N=0,φ=p} for a Stein curve — the statement that makes the syntomic route of §0.6.1 work — is attributed to [19] (Colmez–Dospinescu–Nizioł, ‘Cohomologie des courbes analytiques p-adiques’), listed as ‘en préparation’; and the expectations of Remark 0.3 (iv) about the completed tower are attributed to [21], also ‘en préparation’. The route actually used in the paper (§0.6.2, relative Fontaine rings) is self-contained, and Proposition 3.12 proves the identification for a proper curve, so nothing in the main line depends on [19]; a design job should plan the proper-curve statement and treat the Stein-curve statement as belonging to the companion paper.

Remark 0.3 is a programme, not a set of results: that the theorem should extend to supercuspidal representations of arbitrary weights by replacing Q_p(1) with symmetric powers of the Tate module (ii); that the full G × Ǧ × W_{Q_p}-structure of H^1_ét(M_∞) should have an Emerton-style description through a universal deformation ring (iii); and everything about the completed tower — that m(Π(V)) agrees with Scholze's functor S(Π(V)), that m(Π(V)) ≠ 0 for every absolutely irreducible V of dimension 2, and the factorisations m(Π(V)) = JL_p(V) ⊗ V realising a p-adic Jacquet–Langlands correspondence (iv). Remarks 2.11 and 2.14 likewise only propose Π^an_geo(V_{M,L}) and Π_geo(V_{M,L}) as candidates for a correspondence for GL_2(F) with F ≠ Q_p. None of these may be planned as a target.

The restriction F = Q_p in the main theorem is not cosmetic and Remark 2.6 says exactly where it bites: for a 2-dimensional V with Hom(V, X^+_st(M)) ≠ 0 the admissibility constraints leave only κ_{i,σ} ≥ 0 and Σ_{i,σ} κ_{i,σ} = [F:Q_p], which for F = Q_p forces V = V_{M,L} for a unique line L but for F ≠ Q_p allows other filtrations, including further representations of weights 0 and 1. Everything proved for a general F — Theorems 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and all of §§3–5 — is stated for a general F in the items; only the identification with the p-adic local Langlands correspondence (which needs Proposition 2.9, hence the correspondence itself) is restricted to Q_p. A plan must keep the two apart.

Footnote 3, p. 312, records that Drinfeld stated Proposition 0.1 for the ℓ-adic étale cohomology for every prime ℓ including ℓ = p, but that ‘comme nous l'ont signalé Grosse-Klönne et Berkovich, la preuve de Drinfeld de ce résultat pour ℓ = p laisse beaucoup à désirer’. The paper therefore gives its own proof (Theorem 1.7). A layer that cites Drinfeld's paper for the p-adic statement must cite this one instead; the defect is in a published source and is recorded in the errata log rather than here, since it is not a mistake of this paper.

Remark 4.6 admits that the definitions of O(∂X), Ω^1(∂X) and H^1_c(X,O) used in §4.3.2 are ‘parfaitement ad hoc’, and checks only that they agree with the natural definition — RΓ(∂Z,F) = colim_U RΓ(Z∖U,F) and RΓ_c(Z,F) = cone(RΓ(Z,F) → RΓ(∂Z,F)) — because H^0_c(Z,O) = 0 and H^1(Z,O) = 0 in the cases at hand, the second for the perfectoid tower by a lemma of Kedlaya–Liu. A formalisation should plan the natural definition and prove the comparison, not adopt the ad hoc one.

Three distinct objects are written with almost the same symbol and are genuinely different: M_∞ (the non-completed projective system, whose cohomology is a colimit), M̂_∞ (its completion, a perfectoid space) and the completed cohomology H̃^1_ét(M_∞) — Remark 0.3 (iv) stresses that the last two differ by an interchange of a colimit and a limit, because the M_n are not compact, and that H^1_ét(M̂_∞,L(1)) is ‘beaucoup plus gros’ than H̃^1_ét(M_∞,L(1)). Similarly ~HK(X), HK^1_1(X) and (B^+_st ⊗ H^1_HK(X))^{N=0,φ=p} agree for a proper curve but not for an affinoid, where HK^1_1(X) is not even separated. A plan must name these apart before stating any comparison.
